Can a Dental Implant Shift or Move Over Time?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

If you have recently had a dental implant placed — or you are considering the procedure — it is entirely natural to wonder whether the implant will remain stable for the long term. Some patients notice what feels like slight movement, or they may have heard someone mention that their implant "felt loose," prompting concern and an online search for answers.

Dental implants are designed to integrate firmly with the jawbone through a biological process called osseointegration, which contributes to their long-term stability as a tooth replacement option. However, like any medical or dental treatment, outcomes are influenced by a number of individual factors.

This article explains what causes a dental implant to potentially shift or move, what the warning signs are, what the underlying science tells us, and when it may be appropriate to speak with a dental professional. Understanding these factors can help you make informed decisions about your oral health and feel confident in the care you are receiving.

A successfully integrated dental implant should not move. Dental implant stability depends on osseointegration — the process by which the implant fuses with the jawbone. If a dental implant shifts or feels loose, this may indicate a problem with integration, bone loss, or surrounding gum tissue that warrants professional dental assessment.

What Is a Dental Implant and How Does It Stay in Place?

A dental implant is a small titanium post that is surgically positioned into the jawbone to replace the root of a missing tooth. Once placed, the implant undergoes a healing process during which the surrounding bone tissue gradually bonds with the surface of the titanium post — a process known as osseointegration.

This fusion between bone and implant is what gives dental implants their characteristic stability. Unlike dentures, which rest on the gum surface, or dental bridges, which rely on adjacent teeth for support, a fully integrated implant becomes structurally part of the jaw itself.

Once osseointegration is complete — typically over a period of three to six months, though this varies between individuals — a dental crown or prosthetic tooth is attached to the implant via a connector piece called an abutment. It is this complete assembly — implant, abutment, and crown — that restores the function and appearance of a natural tooth.

For patients researching their options, learning more about dental implant treatment can help clarify what the process involves from consultation through to completion.

The Science Behind Osseointegration

Osseointegration is the biological foundation that makes modern dental implants possible. The term was coined by Swedish orthopaedic researcher Professor Per-Ingvar Brånemark in the 1950s, following observations of how bone tissue could grow directly onto and around titanium surfaces without rejection.

When a titanium implant is placed into prepared bone, the body's natural healing response begins almost immediately. Blood clots form around the implant site, followed by the growth of new bone cells that gradually integrate with the implant surface. Over weeks and months, this new bone matures and hardens, anchoring the implant firmly in position.

The surface texture of modern implants is carefully engineered at a microscopic level to encourage this bone growth. Rough or treated surfaces provide greater contact area and stimulate faster, more thorough osseointegration compared to smooth surfaces used in earlier implant designs.

When osseointegration is successful, the implant should feel and function much like a natural tooth root, with no perceptible movement under normal biting forces. It is only when this biological process is disrupted — or when bone loss occurs at a later stage — that movement may become possible.

Reasons Why a Dental Implant May Shift or Feel Loose

Although a well-integrated dental implant should remain stable, there are several clinical reasons why movement or looseness may be experienced. Understanding these helps patients recognise potential concerns early.

Incomplete osseointegration: In some cases, the implant does not fully integrate with the bone during the initial healing phase. This may be influenced by systemic health conditions, smoking, certain medications, or insufficient bone density at the implant site.

Peri-implantitis: This is a form of gum disease that affects the tissue and bone surrounding a dental implant. Similar to periodontitis around natural teeth, peri-implantitis causes inflammation that can lead to progressive bone loss, destabilising the implant over time.

Bone loss over time: Even after successful osseointegration, the jawbone can gradually resorb due to age, health changes, or ongoing gum disease, reducing the support around the implant.

Loose abutment or crown: Sometimes what feels like implant movement is actually a loose abutment screw or crown — a component issue rather than implant failure itself. This is generally a more straightforward matter to address.

If you are unsure whether the movement is in the crown or the implant itself, this guide to the difference between a loose implant crown and a loose implant fixture can help you understand what to discuss at your appointment.

Traumatic force: Excessive biting forces, teeth grinding (bruxism), or physical trauma may stress the implant-bone interface.

Signs That Your Dental Implant May Need Assessment

Most patients with successful dental implants experience no symptoms of concern. However, there are certain signs that may suggest a professional evaluation is worthwhile.

These include:

  • Noticeable movement or rocking of the implant, crown, or surrounding structure
  • Discomfort or pain around the implant site that persists beyond the normal healing period
  • Swelling, redness, or bleeding around the gum tissue near the implant
  • Difficulty chewing or a change in how your bite feels
  • Receding gum tissue around the implant, which may expose the implant surface
  • A feeling of looseness when touching the crown with your tongue or finger

It is important to note that these symptoms do not necessarily confirm implant failure. A clinical examination is required to determine the cause and appropriate next steps. Seeking advice promptly when something feels unusual is generally in a patient's best interest.

If you are experiencing any of these concerns, a dental professional can assess whether the issue relates to the implant itself, the surrounding tissues, or a component of the restoration.

Peri-Implantitis: The Most Common Threat to Long-Term Implant Stability

Peri-implantitis deserves particular attention because it is one of the most frequently cited causes of implant complications in the longer term. It is a bacterial infection of the soft and hard tissues surrounding a dental implant, which, if left unaddressed, can cause progressive bone loss and ultimately compromise implant stability.

The condition often develops silently in its early stages, with few obvious symptoms beyond some gum redness or bleeding when cleaning. This is why regular dental check-ups and professional hygiene appointments are an important part of caring for dental implants — not only in the months after placement, but on an ongoing basis.

Risk factors for peri-implantitis include a history of gum disease, smoking, poor oral hygiene, poorly controlled diabetes, and a history of periodontitis affecting natural teeth. Patients with these risk factors should discuss them with their dental team as part of their implant care planning.

Maintaining consistent oral hygiene around implants — including brushing, interdental cleaning, and any other tools recommended by your dental professional — is one of the most effective ways to reduce the risk of peri-implantitis developing.

When Professional Dental Assessment May Be Appropriate

If you have a dental implant and notice any changes in how it feels, looks, or functions, it is sensible to arrange an appointment with your dental team rather than waiting to see whether the issue resolves on its own.

If you are deciding how quickly to act, this practical guide on when to see your dentist about a moving implant outlines common warning signs and timing.

In particular, professional evaluation is advisable when:

  • The implant or crown feels different from how it did when first placed
  • You are experiencing persistent discomfort around the implant site
  • There is visible gum change, such as swelling, recession, or redness that does not settle quickly
  • You have noticed a change in your bite or difficulty using that area to chew
  • You are approaching a routine review — regular monitoring of dental implants is part of responsible aftercare

A dentist with implant experience will typically assess the implant using clinical examination and X-rays, which allow visualisation of the bone levels around the implant. This provides important information about integration and stability that cannot be determined from symptoms alone.

Treatment suitability and the most appropriate course of action will always depend on an individual's clinical findings. No online resource, including this article, can provide a personal diagnosis or treatment recommendation.

How to Protect the Long-Term Stability of a Dental Implant

While not every implant complication is preventable, there are several evidence-informed steps patients can take to support the long-term success of their dental implant.

Maintain thorough oral hygiene. Brushing twice daily, cleaning between teeth using interdental brushes or floss, and using any specific cleaning tools recommended for implants helps reduce bacterial accumulation around the implant site.

Attend regular dental check-ups. Routine monitoring allows your dental team to detect early signs of peri-implantitis or bone changes before they progress significantly.

Avoid smoking. Smoking is strongly associated with poorer implant outcomes, including reduced osseointegration rates and higher risk of peri-implantitis. Seeking support to stop smoking before or after implant treatment is generally advisable.

Manage bruxism (teeth grinding). If you grind your teeth, discuss this with your dental team. An occlusal splint may help protect implants and the surrounding bone from excessive forces.

Follow post-operative care advice carefully. The early healing period is particularly important for osseointegration. Following your dental team's specific guidance during this phase supports favourable conditions for successful integration.

Patients who have had implants placed and want to understand how to care for them long term can explore dental implant aftercare and maintenance guidance through reputable clinical resources.

Key Points to Remember

  • A successfully integrated dental implant should not move or shift under normal conditions.
  • Dental implant stability relies on osseointegration — the fusion of the titanium implant with the jawbone.
  • If an implant feels loose or movement is noticed, this requires professional assessment; it does not always mean implant failure.
  • Peri-implantitis is a significant cause of implant instability and is associated with bone loss around the implant site.
  • Regular dental check-ups, good oral hygiene, and not smoking all support long-term implant health.
  • Treatment suitability and outcomes vary between individuals and can only be assessed during a clinical examination.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it normal for a new dental implant to feel slightly different at first?

During the healing period following implant placement, some patients notice a degree of unfamiliarity or mild discomfort around the site. This is generally associated with post-surgical healing rather than implant movement. However, if discomfort persists, worsens, or you notice any mobility in the implant, it is always worth contacting your dental team to have this checked. Early assessment is always preferable to waiting.

Can a loose dental crown mean the implant itself has failed?

Not necessarily. What feels like a loose implant may in some cases be a loose abutment screw or crown rather than a problem with the implant fixture itself. This is a relatively common issue and is often straightforward to address. A clinical assessment is needed to distinguish between a component issue and a problem with the implant's integration with the bone. It is always worth seeking professional advice rather than assuming the worst.

How long do dental implants typically last?

Dental implants are designed to be a long-term tooth replacement solution, and with appropriate care and regular dental monitoring, many implants remain stable for many years. However, individual outcomes depend on factors including oral hygiene, general health, bone quality, and lifestyle choices such as smoking. No specific outcome can be guaranteed, and your dental team will discuss realistic expectations based on your individual circumstances during consultation.

Can gum disease affect a dental implant?

Yes. Gum disease, particularly a condition called peri-implantitis, can affect the tissues and bone surrounding a dental implant, potentially leading to bone loss and implant instability over time. Patients with a history of gum disease should ensure this is well managed before and after implant treatment, and should maintain consistent oral hygiene and regular professional monitoring. Discussing your history of gum disease with your dental team is important when considering a dental implant consultation.

Does grinding teeth affect dental implants?

Teeth grinding, known as bruxism, can place excessive force on dental implants, the surrounding bone, and the implant crown. This may increase the risk of implant complications over time. If you are aware that you grind your teeth, or if your dental team has identified signs of bruxism during examination, it is important to discuss this prior to implant treatment. An occlusal splint or night guard may be recommended to help protect the implant from damaging forces during sleep.

What should I do if I think my dental implant is moving?

If you believe your dental implant or the crown attached to it is moving, the most appropriate step is to contact your dental practice to arrange an assessment. Avoid applying pressure to the area or attempting to adjust anything yourself. A clinical examination, which may include dental X-rays, will allow your dental team to determine the cause of the movement and advise on the most appropriate course of action. Do not delay seeking advice if you have concerns.

Conclusion

A well-placed and properly integrated dental implant should remain stable and secure, functioning comfortably as part of your everyday life. The process of osseointegration — through which the implant fuses with the jawbone — is the biological foundation of implant stability, and when it is successful, patients often report that their implant feels indistinguishable from a natural tooth.

That said, various factors can influence long-term implant stability, including gum health, bone density, lifestyle choices, and how diligently an individual maintains their oral hygiene and attends regular dental check-ups. Being aware of these factors, and knowing the signs that may warrant a dental assessment, is part of being an informed patient.

If you notice any changes in how your dental implant feels or functions — whether it is movement, discomfort, gum changes, or difficulty chewing — seeking professional advice is always the recommended course of action. Early assessment can make a meaningful difference to outcomes.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.
